Mom! Dad! Check your phones! Now!
It's 6 a.m. Your phone won't stop buzzing. You open your bank app. You blink. You look again.
One million dollars. In your account. Yesterday you had twelve dollars and a coupon for free fries.
You run downstairs. Dad is staring at his phone. Mom is staring at hers. Your little sister is staring at hers.
This has to be a mistake. Banks don't just do this.
It's on the news. Everybody got it. Every single person on Earth. One million dollars. Overnight.
Nobody knows where it came from. Nobody cares. You're rich. Everyone is rich.
So, what happens next? Day one is amazing. Day two is weird. And by day thirty... well. Let's see.
Day one. Your street looks like a car show. Your neighbor bought a sports car. In pink.
The guy across the street bought three. He can only drive one at a time. He doesn't care.
Dad orders a boat. You don't live near water.
It's for the driveway. It's a driveway boat.
I don't need to swim. I'm a millionaire.
You buy every game ever made. Plus a gaming chair that cost more than your old house.
It has massage, cooling, and a tiny fridge in the armrest. You will never leave this chair.
I bought a horse. He's in the backyard. His name is Mister Pancake.
Mister Pancake eats Mom's flowers. Then the fence. Then the doormat.
Who sold a seven-year-old a horse?
Day two. You go to school. Nobody else does. Not even the teacher.
There's a note on the door. "Gone to Hawaii. Forever."
You sit alone in an empty classroom for ten minutes. Just to feel it. Then you go home and play games for nine hours.
Dad goes to work out of habit. The office is empty. His boss is wearing a crown.
I quit. You quit. Everybody quit.
Who cares? I'm buying an island. A small one. Okay, a medium one.
And that's the problem. Nobody wants to work anymore. Not the bus driver. Not the cook. Not the guy who fixes the internet.
Day three. The garbage truck doesn't come. Neither does the mail. Or the pizza guy.
Your street now has seven sports cars, one boat, one horse, and a mountain of trash bags.
Somebody should really pick that up.
Everybody looks at somebody else. Nobody picks it up.
By the end of the day, the trash pile is taller than the boat. A family of raccoons moves in. They look very happy.
Day four. You turn on the TV. A famous movie star is crying on the news.
Nobody wants her autograph anymore. Everyone already has a mansion. Being rich isn't special when everybody is.
Huh. I feel kind of bad for her.
I don't. I have a horse.
Day five. The internet goes down. Your sister screams like the world is ending.
Dad calls a repair guy. The repair guy is also a millionaire. He's on a yacht. He laughs. He hangs up.
Dad calls ten more. Same answer. One of them is on the same yacht.
Okay. How hard can it be? I'll fix it myself.
Dad unplugs the router. Plugs it back in. Unplugs it again. Now the TV is broken too.
Day seven. Mom goes to the store for milk. A carton of milk now costs fifty dollars.
The cashier shrugs. Everyone has a million dollars, so the store raised the prices. Then raised them again.
By lunch it's a hundred dollars. By dinner, two hundred. The price tags change while you're looking at them.
I'll just take one banana. How much is one banana?
The cashier says a number. Mom puts the banana back very, very slowly.
Day eight. Mom has had enough. Tonight, the family goes to the fanciest restaurant in town. The one with the tiny food on big plates.
The doors are open. The candles are lit. And there's nobody inside. No waiter. No chef. Nobody.
Hello? We're millionaires! We'd like a table!
Nobody answers. So Dad walks into the kitchen and puts on the chef's hat.
Forty minutes later, the smoke alarm goes off. Dinner is cereal. Fancy cereal. On a very big plate.
This is the best restaurant ever.
On the way out, Dad leaves a tip. One million dollars. There's nobody there to take it.
And here's the crazy part. This has really happened. Not with free money, but with too much money.
In Zimbabwe, the government printed so much money that prices went up every single day. Sometimes twice a day.
In 2009, the country printed a single bill worth one hundred trillion dollars. And it still couldn't buy a week of groceries.
So being a millionaire is only cool if nobody else is?
Pretty much. Money is only worth something when there isn't too much of it.
Day ten. Dad holds a family meeting. He has a spreadsheet. Nobody asked for a spreadsheet.
The boat was two hundred thousand. The horse was fifty thousand. The gaming chair was... how much was the gaming chair?
I don't want to talk about the gaming chair.
And milk is now five hundred dollars.
And the stores are running out. The trucks stopped coming. Truck drivers are millionaires too.
The shelves get emptier every day. First the snacks. Then the bread. Then the toilet paper.
Day fourteen. The lights go out. The whole city. Pitch black.
The people who run the power plant? You guessed it. Island. Yacht. Hawaii.
I can't charge my phone. What do I do?
When I was a kid, we played board games.
So you play a board game. By candlelight. It's called Monopoly. Nobody finds it funny.
Day sixteen. Dad wakes up with a toothache. A big one. His face looks like a balloon.
I'll pay any dentist ten thousand dollars. Twenty thousand!
Ten thousand dollars now buys about three apples. Every dentist in town is on vacation.
Then Grandma shows up. With a piece of string and a door.
Grandma ties one end to the tooth. And the other end to the door. She doesn't count to three.
The door slams. The tooth is out. Dad is fine. Mostly.
How much do I owe you?
Grandma wants one thing. A loaf of bread. And for the first time, you realize: bread might be worth more than a million dollars.
Day twenty. The pink sports car is out of gas. The gas station is closed. The guy who owns it is on vacation.
The whole street is full of expensive cars. None of them move. Everybody walks.
And for the first time in weeks, people start talking to each other. About something weird.
Who still knows how to do stuff?
Turns out, a lot of people do. Your neighbor can fix pipes. Grandma can bake bread. The quiet guy at number twelve can fix the power.
Your sister can ride a horse. That's suddenly very useful.
Nobody pays with money anymore. You trade. Bread for a pipe fix. Horse rides for eggs. Dad trades the boat for six chickens.
Mister Pancake is the richest one in the family now.
Day twenty-five. Your teacher comes back from Hawaii. She's sunburned and broke.
I spent it on a coconut.
It was a really good coconut. Now open your books.
And you know what? You're kind of happy to be back at school. Don't tell anyone.
Then she hands out homework. Okay. A little less happy.
Dad goes back to the office. His boss is there too. No crown this time.
The island didn't have Wi-Fi. Or food. Or a toilet.
Dad sits down at his desk. Two hundred and forty emails. He has never been this happy to see them.
Day thirty. Your family sits at the kitchen table. The boat is gone. The gaming chair is firewood.
We had a million dollars and now we're poorer than before.
At least we still have the horse.
And you learned something. Money doesn't make bread. People make bread. Money is just how we say thank you.
Then, at midnight, every phone on Earth buzzes again. A new message.
"Thanks for testing. Round two starts tomorrow. This time, only one person gets the money."
Your phone buzzes one more time. It says, "Congratulations."
